clue.text: Old money with rates by 18 6

definitions.note: the word that follows Rates of in a Malcolm Bradbury title

explanation.surface: Talk of pre-decimal money and the rates charged by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 6 is the novelist Malcolm Bradbury, who wrote Rates of Exchange; this is one of a set of clues built on his titles.
explanation.definitionFit: Bradbury's 1983 novel is called Rates of Exchange, so this word completes the title alongside rates.

clue.text: Cover a scene of confusion

indicators.note: a scene of confusion is a muddle, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: the six letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A cover-up during a scene of chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: To encase something is to enclose it in a covering or shell.

clue.text: Dog on wheels, red for honoured guest

definitions.note: the thing that goes with red, rolled out for a VIP

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece placed on another follows it, so the wheels come first here

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car
a dog is a typical pet

explanation.surface: A dog on a little wheeled cart, given the red-carpet treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: A red carpet is rolled out to welcome a distinguished visitor, so this word follows red.

clue.text: Take (more or less) a letter? Indeed

definitions.meaning: the surface reads like a boss asking a secretary to take dictation
the setter's reading: to receive a letter and agree to it, as one would a bill or an offer, is to say yes

explanation.surface: An office scene: will you, more or less, take a letter? Yes indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: A whimsical Araucaria clue: the answer is a near-sound of except, and saying yes to a letter's offer is agreeing to it.
explanation.definitionFit: To take what is offered, such as a gift or a proposal, is to agree to receive it.

clue.text: Bird, in French then in Greek, gaining height

indicators.note: gaining means taking on an extra piece at the end
in says the French word for then sits inside the French word for Greek

parts.note: grec is the French word for Greek, 'in French' governing it too
enfin is French for then, or at last

explanation.surface: A bird is named in French and then Greek while it climbs higher.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words come from French: the second 'in' places one inside the other, and 'gaining' adds the height letter at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: This common European songbird has olive-yellow plumage and a heavy seed-cracking bill.

clue.text: Acting A for Alan is subsiding

indicators.note: for means one thing stands in place of another

parts.note: acting points to the English actor Alan Bates
the actor's first name, taken as written

explanation.surface: An acting grade of A given to someone called Alan is slowly falling.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Bates was an English stage and film actor; replace his first name with A.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm or fever that abates dies down, which is what subsiding means.

clue.text: See 18
Article taken from experimental novel with three horns?

definitions.note: describes a dilemma with three horns, i.e. this noun

indicators.note: taken from means removed, so the article comes out of the following word

parts.note: Emma is the Jane Austen novel

explanation.surface: An avant-garde novel that removes its articles and features something three-horned.
explanation.walkthrough: A dilemma has two horns, so a choice with three is a trilemma.
explanation.definitionFit: A trilemma is a difficult choice among three options, a dilemma with an extra horn.

clue.text: Observation of model in the course of expressing regret

indicators.note: something happening in the course of an action sits inside it

explanation.surface: Noticing a fashion model while sighing with regret.
explanation.walkthrough: The Model T was Ford's famous early car, so model often gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: A sighting is an instance of seeing something, a recorded observation.

clue.text: Many divine voices have little craft

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number

explanation.surface: A crowd of prophets with only small boats.
explanation.walkthrough: Many giving C, the Roman hundred, is a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Coracles are small round boats of wicker and hide, so they are little craft.

clue.text: It's wrong, according to 18 6, to give apple to genie

definitions.note: the first part of the title Eating People is Wrong

indicators.note: to give is to yield or bend, so the letters that follow lose their shape

explanation.surface: A moral warning against handing fruit to a genie, echoing Eve's apple.
explanation.walkthrough: Eating People is Wrong was Malcolm Bradbury's first novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bradbury's 1959 campus novel is titled Eating People is Wrong, so this phrase is what he says is wrong.

clue.text: Going gradually (and fatally?) "Ho!" is 18 6's

parts.note: to go west is to die, and the word precedes Ho! in the Kingsley title

explanation.surface: Someone advancing slowly, perhaps to their death, with a cry of Ho!
explanation.walkthrough: Westward Ho! is Charles Kingsley's novel; Bradbury's 1965 novel is Stepping Westward. Going west is slang for dying, hence fatally.
explanation.definitionFit: Stepping Westward is the title of Malcolm Bradbury's second novel, about a British writer in America.

clue.text: Not want a thing?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to raise an objection, disapprove
second meaning: an item or article

explanation.walkthrough: Pronounced differently, the verb and the noun share their spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to oppose something; as a noun it means a material item.

clue.text: Even more deplorable, slower list must be used

indicators.note: the letters must be put to use in another arrangement

explanation.surface: Complaining that a slower list being imposed makes things more deplorable.
explanation.definitionFit: Still worse means worse yet, going beyond something already bad.

clue.text: 18 6 got his new model army, not turned out

indicators.note: a new model of something is a reworked version, so these letters are rebuilt
turned out suggests the letters are tipped out and set down differently

explanation.surface: Someone took charge of Cromwell's New Model Army, which was then not mustered.
explanation.walkthrough: Cromwell's New Model Army was Parliament's force in the English Civil War; the famous phrase is split so 'new model' and 'turned out' both signal rearrangement. 'got' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-referenced lights name the figure this title describes, the satirical campus novel's sociologist hero.

clue.text: One drunkard starts (or drinks like this) — they could be radioactive

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drinker
ope is a poetic form of open, to start

explanation.surface: A drunk beginning to drink, glowing as though radioactive.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket offers a second parse: I plus SO (like this) plus TOPES (drinks heavily).
explanation.definitionFit: Isotopes are forms of an element differing in neutron count, and some decay emitting radiation.

clue.text: No charge for stowing such property as cargo?

parts.note: a ship's hold is where cargo is stowed

explanation.surface: Asking whether stowing goods as cargo is free of charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the joke that property held outright is like cargo in a hold carried for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Freehold is property owned outright and permanently, as opposed to leasehold.

clue.text: Edentate from African country dropping tail into cask

indicators.note: going into something places it inside

parts.note: a pin is a small cask holding about four gallons

indicators.note: losing its tail means the final letter goes

explanation.surface: A toothless creature from Africa that tumbles into a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: A pin is an old cask size, half a firkin.
explanation.definitionFit: Pangolins, scaly anteaters lacking teeth, were classed among the edentates.

clue.text: Literary giant and teacher arranged dumb crambo rally

parts.note: schoolchildren address a male teacher as sir

indicators.note: when things are arranged they are set in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A famous writer and a schoolmaster organising a party game of dumb crambo.
explanation.walkthrough: Dumb crambo is a parlour game of miming rhymes.
explanation.definitionFit: The knighted novelist and critic, author of The History Man, was a major literary figure.

clue.text: Loner to inherit a thousand

indicators.note: added to the word, the thousand goes inside it

parts.note: the word without its opening two letters, a preposition
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A recluse about to come into a fortune of a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: Inherit loses its in, then the thousand goes in the middle; Bradbury's novel To the Hermitage lurks in to and this answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit lives alone in seclusion, the archetypal solitary person.

clue.text: A good start and finish for a business

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Advice on how a company should begin and end well.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda lists the items of business to be dealt with at a meeting.

clue.text: A theologian was the guide, which is bad

explanation.surface: A clergyman acted as a guide, and things went badly.
explanation.walkthrough: DD, Doctor of Divinity, is the standard crossword theologian.
explanation.definitionFit: An addled egg has gone rotten, so addled can mean bad or spoiled.

clue.text: Silver in solver: 18 6 got to 19 in it

definitions.meaning: to a solver, silver suggests the era that follows it in Silver Age, or simply grey-haired years
Bradbury's novel To the Hermitage: put the 19 answer inside these words and the title appears

explanation.walkthrough: Insert HERMIT into this answer to get THE HERMITAGE, the destination in Bradbury's 2000 novel To the Hermitage.
explanation.definitionFit: The Silver Age is a classical era, so silver is a descriptive label for the period.

clue.text: Very cutting, but inviting riposte

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sharp on both sides, doubly sharp
second meaning: an argument that can be turned back against its user

explanation.walkthrough: Cuts is also a Bradbury novella, a nod to the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A blade sharpened on both sides cuts doubly, and a remark that cuts both ways lays itself open to retort.

clue.text: See 10
It's wrong for 18 6's doctor with English ending

indicators.note: the doctor's name differs only by its final English letter, which is shed here

parts.note: Doctor Criminale is a Bradbury novel

explanation.surface: Something being called wrong in a Bradbury novel about a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Criminale (1992) is Bradbury's novel; his name is this word with E at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminal is used loosely as a synonym for disgraceful or morally wrong.

clue.text: 5's clue's not main line

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step

explanation.surface: A railway term borrowed from a neighbouring clue, with the main line set aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue 5 ends with subsiding; drop its first three letters and the answer remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A siding is a short railway track off the running line, used for shunting or parking.
